title: English was the language I built my career in. In Canada, it became something to prove

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·First Person

Anusuya Datta had never given a second thought to knowing English, having always written and spoken in the language. After moving to Saskatchewan, people continually remarked on her English skills, both in complimentary and derogatory ways.
After moving to Canada, people kept reminding me English was my second language
· for CBC First Person
· Posted: Nov 15, 2026 4:00 AM EST | Last Updated: 7 hours ago
This First Person column is written by Anusuya Datta, a writer and journalist based in Saskatoon. For more information about First Person stories, see the FAQ.
I had only been in Canada for two weeks when I got the question that would follow me around for the next few years.
I’d gone to the pharmacy to ask about medication. The woman behind the counter looked up and said, “You speak very good English.”
By then, I had spent more than 15 years earning my living in English. Now I was being congratulated for successfully asking about a prescription.
“Thank you,” I said.
“Where did you learn it?”
“In India.”
She looked impressed.
I walked out with my prescription and a piece of information: in Canada, my English was an accomplishment.
Anusuya Datta attends a space conference, posing with a therapeutic robot seal proposed as a companion for astronauts on long missions. (Submitted by Anusuya Datta)

I had assumed I was the one immigrating. It turned out there were two of us. My English had done its paperwork. Canada makes you declare your English. That's what the international English language test is for. My English did very well. We both assumed that was the end of it. But someone had forgotten to send Saskatchewan a copy.

English wasn't the first language I learned, I admit. But it was the one I was educated in. I read novels in it and did a master's in it. Nobody in India ever congratulated me on it. It was like having elbows. You don't get complimented on elbows.
Coming face-to-face with assumptions

The pharmacist wasn’t the last. Neighbours told me I spoke English well. Doctors told me. People in shops told me, with the warmth usually reserved for someone who has parallel parked a combine. They were being kind to a newcomer, and I was grateful. I still am.
I said thank you. Every time. You don't hold up the queue to explain English isn't rocket science, and that you have, in fact, explained rocket science in it.
I have an accent when I speak English
Then my English got a job. So did I, at the same tech company in Saskatoon, which was convenient. We were both hired at a junior level. That seemed fair. We were new.

Soon my English was fine-tuning everyone's copy. Colleagues sent me their drafts the way you send a shirt to the dry cleaner, without conversation and expecting it back clean. My English had become the office Wi-Fi. Everyone used it. You don’t promote the Wi-Fi.
Eventually, I brought up a promotion on a call with my boss. I was told it was too soon. I didn't have the necessary experience.
“You need to be patient. These things take time,” he repeated, a little too slowly, as if he were weighing my English comprehension skills.
After the call, I sat for a long time. What my English lacked, I understood, was Canadian experience. It had only the other kind, where you do the work.
A year later, I joined an agriculture-technology company. I imagined data and software. The company sold agricultural chemicals in jugs.

This isn’t an attack on chemicals. Chemicals have had a long and successful career in agriculture. Jugs, for their part, have performed admirably throughout human civilization. But I couldn’t understand how the company involved technology.

The company wanted lots of content, the kind that sounds like the future of food. So I asked what the technology was. In my line of work, this is a standard opening question. It turned out to be a hostile act.
I was given a few words. Innovation. Sustainability. Transformation. None was attached to anything. My job was to expand them. I asked for details. I was told to read up.

So I read everything I could find and came back with questions. The boss came back with more keywords. Then the words started changing their meaning. One week, sustainability was the next big thing. The next, it was “woke.”

Finally, I asked why he was saying the exact opposite of what he’d said the week before. That was when he explained the problem. I wasn't understanding his feedback because English wasn't my first language.

The second half was true. I couldn’t fault his research, but it came a little late. My English had been excellent while it produced adjectives. It developed problems the moment it produced question marks.
“I’ve written for American and European organizations for over 15 years,” I told him. “My English has never been a problem. Until now.”

items: I'm fluent in English, but my accent still feels like a barrier to acceptance

blocks.text: I was angry. Of all the things I expected to have to prove in Canada, my English wasn’t on the list.
I ended up leaving the company. My English came with me. We had been through a lot together.
It’s been more than two years since. The bitterness has aged nicely, like cheddar.

Meanwhile, my English and I went freelance. Not one client told me my English was so good. Or so bad. They asked for a redraft when one was needed and sent more work. I recommend this as a form of compliment. It’s quieter and you can invoice for it.

These days I work for a global company with people in Canada, the U.S. and Europe. People here have opinions, too. They tell me when a piece is great and when I’ve got the technology totally wrong. Not one of them has an opinion about my English. A plumber is judged on the pipes. Nobody asks where the wrench is from. I've never been so happily criticized.
English is still not my first language. It's still doing very well. It even has Canadian experience now.
Thank you for asking.

ABOUT THE AUTHOR

A journalist based in Saskatoon, Anusuya has a keen interest in connecting technology with sustainability and social causes, and writes for various tech media platforms. She has also delivered guest lectures at the University of British Columbia’s school of journalism on the use of satellite imagery in storytelling.
